summary: Final source-only contribution, aimed at the axis the main finding sits on. Reading the other branch of the same lease test the MsgForgetLeader gap partly defeats turned up a second, deliberate way past it. The suppression is written as force := bytes.Equal(m.GetContext(), []byte(campaignTransfer)), and a higher-term MsgVote or MsgPreVote is ignored only when force is false and inLease holds — so a request carrying that marker is answered: the receiver advances to the higher term, becomes a follower with no leader, and then evaluates canVote and isUpToDate instead of honouring its lease. The marker is attached by campaign() only when the campaign is a transfer (t == campaignTransfer), the path reached from stepFollower's MsgTimeoutNow case via r.hup(campaignTransfer); that campaign increments the term, sends MsgVote rather than MsgPreVote, and is the only producer of that context value in the snapshot. Because the receiver keeps no local record of a pending transfer and the context field is neither authenticated nor compared with anything, it cannot distinguish a real transfer from a claimed one. I recorded the mechanism as one behaviour entry with precise anchors (raft.go:1067-1071, 1758-1763, plus the existing lease anchors), added those two sources, and registered one question, @lease_transfer_bypass, whose discriminator settles the empirical half in a single probe: the same up-to-date higher-term MsgPreVote delivered twice to a follower with a live lease, once bare and once with the CampaignTransfer context. I deliberately did not assert a defect: the marker is a claim about an internal precondition, so judging it a defect would contradict the same reasoning that already refuted the term-zero boundary unless the snapshot is shown to place a verification duty on the receiver — the question records that as the expected landing so a continuation is not tempted to overread it. No experiment was filed, so nothing is left uncited, and the update validates with execution_requested=false. The net effect is that a reviewer assessing how strong the CheckQuorum lease really is now finds both of its exits side by side: the one the run measured with receipts, and the one the sources show.
